title: The Great Day of the LORD Is Near
summary: In the days of King Josiah, God announces through Zephaniah that he will sweep away everything from the face of the earth, beginning with Judah and Jerusalem. He targets those who worship Baal and the stars, who swear by the LORD and by Milcom, the royal officials who adopt foreign ways, the violent and deceitful, and the complacent who think the LORD will do nothing. The chapter ends with a description of the great Day of the LORD as a day of wrath, darkness, and battle cry, from which neither silver nor gold can deliver.
story: The prophets of the eighth century (Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, Micah) warned Israel and Judah, and Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC. Judah survived, but under King Manasseh in the seventh century it sank into the worst idolatry in its history. Zephaniah speaks to the generation that inherited Manasseh's legacy, in the reign of his grandson Josiah. The chapter's announcement of judgment explains why Jerusalem would eventually fall, and its picture of the Day of the LORD takes up a theme that Amos had introduced (Amos 5:18-20) and gives it its fullest form. Chapter 2 will call the humble to seek the LORD before that day comes, and chapter 3 will look beyond it to restoration.
historical:
Josiah became king about 640 BC, at the age of eight, after the assassination of his father Amon (2 Kings 21:23-24). His grandfather Manasseh had reigned for fifty-five years and filled Judah with foreign worship: altars to Baal, an Asherah pole in the temple, altars to the host of heaven in the temple courts, and child sacrifice (2 Kings 21:1-9). Josiah began a sweeping reform, which 2 Chronicles 34 dates from his twelfth year (about 628 BC) and 2 Kings 22 to 23 centers on his eighteenth year (about 622 BC), when the Book of the Law was found in the temple. Zephaniah 1 describes practices that reform targeted: the remnant of Baal, the idolatrous priests (the same rare word appears in 2 Kings 23:5), worship of the host of heaven on rooftops (2 Kings 23:12), and worship of Milcom, the god of the Ammonites (2 Kings 23:13). Most scholars therefore date this chapter before the reform or in its early years.

The international scene was shifting. Assyria, which had dominated Judah for a century, was weakening after the reign of Ashurbanipal, and Babylon and the Medes were rising. Older scholarship sometimes linked the invader behind Zephaniah's warnings to Scythian raiders mentioned by the Greek historian Herodotus, but that view has largely been abandoned; the chapter names no enemy and presents the coming judgment as the LORD's own act. In hindsight, Judah's first readers after 587 or 586 BC would have heard in it the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem.
cultural:
The chapter's list of offenses gives a vivid picture of Jerusalem's religious life. Flat rooftops were used for many purposes in the ancient Near East, including worship of the sun, moon, and stars, a practice associated with Assyrian influence. Swearing by the LORD and by Milcom shows syncretism, an attempt to keep the God of Israel while adding other gods. Foreign apparel (verse 8) may refer to royal officials adopting the clothing of foreign courts or cults as a sign of divided loyalty. Leaping over the threshold (verse 9) is obscure; 1 Samuel 5:5 records that the priests of the Philistine god Dagon avoided stepping on the threshold of his temple, and some think Zephaniah refers to a similar superstition, while others think it means servants rushing into houses to plunder them for their masters.

Verses 10 and 11 name districts of Jerusalem. The Fish Gate was on the north side of the city, probably where fish from the coast or Galilee were sold. The Second District (Mishneh) was a newer quarter, also mentioned as the home of the prophetess Huldah (2 Kings 22:14). The Hollow (Maktesh, literally mortar) was probably a low-lying market area where merchants weighed silver. Wine left on its dregs (verse 12, rendered settled in complacency) thickens and becomes syrupy if it is not poured off; the image describes people grown sluggish and self-satisfied.
literary: The chapter is built in widening and narrowing circles. It begins with the whole earth (verses 2 and 3), narrows to Judah and Jerusalem (verses 4 to 6), then to specific groups and places within the city (verses 7 to 13), before widening again to a cosmic description of the Day of the LORD (verses 14 to 18). The opening echoes the flood and reverses the order of creation in Genesis 1: humans, beasts, birds, fish. Verse 7 introduces the image of the day as a sacrifice to which God has invited guests, with the chilling twist that Judah is the sacrifice. Verses 15 and 16 contain a series of six day of phrases, the first a single word and the rest in pairs (wrath, trouble and distress, destruction and desolation, darkness and gloom, clouds and blackness, horn blast and battle cry). In the Latin Vulgate, verse 15 begins dies irae, dies illa, and those words gave their name to the medieval hymn Dies irae, traditionally attributed to Thomas of Celano in the thirteenth century and long sung in the Latin requiem mass.

outline.t: Heading: Zephaniah in the days of Josiah
God will sweep away all creation
Judgment on Baal worship and divided loyalty
The LORD's sacrifice: officials and the violent
Wailing in Jerusalem's markets; the complacent punished
The great day: wrath, darkness, and no ransom

doctrines.note: The Day of the LORD is God's decisive act to judge sin, near in Zephaniah's time and pointing to a final day. It falls first on God's own people, because privilege brings accountability.
The chapter condemns Baal worship, astral worship, and divided loyalty that swears by the LORD and by Milcom. It also counts turning away and not seeking the LORD as idolatry's quieter form.
Those who say the LORD will do nothing, either good or bad, deny that God acts in history. Zephaniah insists that God sees, searches Jerusalem with lamps, and acts.

words.note: Yom, day, used fifteen times in this chapter, as often as the divine name itself. The Day of the LORD is not a twenty-four-hour period but the time of God's decisive action. Zephaniah strings together day of wrath, day of trouble, day of darkness, so that the word itself becomes a drumbeat of approaching judgment.

Qarov, near, used three times (verses 7 and 14). The Day of the LORD is not a distant theory but imminent. The prophets consistently speak of it as near, calling for response now, even when its final fulfillment lies further ahead.

Shemer, dregs or lees, the sediment in wine. Verse 12 literally speaks of men thickening on their dregs, which the BSB renders settled in complacency. Wine left undisturbed on its sediment grows thick and sluggish; so do people who assume God will never act.

Qin'ah, jealousy or zeal. Verse 18 speaks of the fire of His jealousy. God's jealousy is his passionate commitment to his rightful claim on his people and his world, aroused here by their devotion to other gods.

christ: The Day of the LORD is one of the Old Testament themes the New Testament takes up most directly. Early Christians spoke of the day of the Lord as the day of Jesus Christ's return (1 Corinthians 1:8, 1 Thessalonians 5:2, 2 Peter 3:10), and they used Zephaniah's imagery of darkness, trumpet blast, and the failure of wealth to save. Jesus' own warnings about sudden judgment, in which people eat, drink, buy, sell, plant, and build until the day comes (Luke 17:26-30), echo verse 13's picture of houses built but not inhabited and vineyards planted but not enjoyed. The chapter also sets up the question the gospel answers: if neither silver nor gold can deliver on the day of wrath, what can? The New Testament answers that believers are redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19). That is a thematic connection, not a prediction in Zephaniah, but it shows how the New Testament hears this chapter.

hard.q: Why does God threaten to sweep away all creation, animals included, when humans are the ones who sinned?
hard.a: The opening verses deliberately echo the flood and the order of creation in Genesis 1, and the language is intentionally sweeping. Several readings help. Many interpreters understand the universal language as prophetic hyperbole, meant to convey the seriousness of judgment rather than a literal prediction that all animals would die. The immediate focus narrows quickly to Judah and Jerusalem. Others point out that in the Bible, human sin damages the whole creation (Genesis 3:17, Romans 8:20-22), so judgment on humanity inevitably affects the world humans were meant to care for. The later chapters also show that the purpose of judgment is not annihilation but purification: a remnant remains and the nations come to worship. Readers still feel the severity of the passage, and rightly so; it is meant to shake complacency.

questions: Some in Jerusalem said the LORD will do nothing, either good or bad. In what ways do people, including religious people, live as though God is uninvolved?
Zephaniah condemns those who swear by the LORD and by Milcom. What divided loyalties are most tempting for you?
Verse 18 says silver and gold cannot deliver on the day of wrath. What do people trust to protect them that would fail in a real crisis?
